meta.chapterTitle: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
meta.topicIdHint: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
meta.chapter: System of Particles and Rotational Motion

learningOutcomes: Locate the centre of mass of discrete and continuous (symmetric) bodies, and use Newton's second law for a system of particles, MA = F_ext.
Compute the vector (cross) product of two vectors and use it to define torque and angular momentum.
Apply v = ω × r, τ = r × F and l = r × p, and relate torque to the rate of change of angular momentum, dL/dt = τ.
State the conditions for translational and rotational equilibrium of a rigid body, apply the principle of moments (levers), and locate the centre of gravity.
Compute moment of inertia using the parallel axis theorem and the standard results table, and apply τ = Iα and L = Iω for rotation about a fixed axis.
Apply the rotational kinematics equations and rolling-without-slipping condition, including the total kinetic energy of a rolling body.

cheatSheet.oneLiner: Centre of mass & momentum of a system → vector products, torque & angular momentum → equilibrium & centre of gravity → moment of inertia → rotational kinematics/dynamics → rolling motion.
mustKnowBullets: Centre of mass: R = Σm_i r_i / M (discrete); X=(1/M)∫x dm etc. for continuous bodies; coincides with the geometric centre for uniform symmetric bodies.
Motion of CM: M A = F_ext — the CM moves as if all the mass were concentrated there and all external forces acted there; internal forces never affect it.
Total momentum P = MV; if F_ext = 0, P is conserved and the CM moves with constant velocity (or stays at rest).
Vector product: a×b has magnitude ab sinθ, direction by the right-hand screw rule; a×b = −(b×a) (NOT commutative); a×a = 0.
v = ω × r relates the linear velocity of a particle of a rotating rigid body to its angular velocity and position vector.
Torque τ = r × F; torque vanishes if r=0, F=0, or θ=0°/180° (force line passes through the origin).
Angular momentum of a particle l = r × p; dl/dt = τ (rotational analogue of F=dp/dt).
For a system: dL/dt = τ_ext (internal torques cancel in pairs by Newton's third law); if τ_ext=0, L is conserved — classic examples: ice skater/diver pulling in arms speeds up spin.
Rigid body equilibrium needs BOTH: ΣF=0 (translational) AND Στ=0 (rotational) — a couple has ΣF=0 but Στ≠0, so it rotates without translating.
Principle of moments (lever): d₁F₁ = d₂F₂; Mechanical Advantage = F₁/F₂ = d₂/d₁.
Centre of gravity is the point where the total gravitational torque is zero; it coincides with the centre of mass whenever g is uniform over the body.
Moment of inertia I = Σm_i r_i²  (r_i ⊥ distance from axis); radius of gyration k defined by I = Mk².
Parallel axis theorem: I = I_cm + Md² (d = distance between the two parallel axes).
Rotational kinematics (constant α): ω=ω₀+αt, θ=ω₀t+½αt², ω²=ω₀²+2αθ — exact analogues of the linear equations with x→θ, v→ω, a→α.
Rotational dynamics: τ=Iα (Newton's 2nd law for rotation); Work W=τΔθ; Power P=τω; Rotational KE K=½Iω².
Rolling without slipping: v_cm=ωR, a_cm=αR; total KE = ½mv² + ½Iω² (translation + rotation, NEVER just one term).

highlights.text: The centre of mass of a system of particles is the point at which the total mass of the system may be thought to be concentrated for describing its translational motion. For a symmetric homogeneous body it coincides with the geometric centre.
highlights.whyItMatters: Foundation for treating extended bodies as an effective single particle for translational purposes.

highlights.text: The centre of mass need not lie inside the body — e.g. for a ring, a horseshoe, or an L-shaped lamina it can fall outside the material itself.

The centre of mass of a system moves as though all the mass of the system is concentrated there and all the external forces act at that point: M A = F_ext. Internal forces (action-reaction pairs) never affect the motion of the centre of mass.
highlights.whyItMatters: Explains why an exploding projectile's fragments' CM continues along the original parabolic path, and why a person walking on a frictionless trolley shifts their own position but the trolley+person CM stays fixed.

highlights.text: Total linear momentum of a system P = MV. If the total external force on a system is zero, the total linear momentum is conserved, i.e. P = constant — this is the law of conservation of momentum for a system of particles, generalising the two-body case.
highlights.whyItMatters: Basis of binary-star, radioactive-decay-recoil and explosion-in-flight problems where internal forces are large but external forces are absent/negligible.

highlights.text: The vector (cross) product is NOT commutative: a×b = −(b×a). Both a×b and b×a have the same magnitude but opposite directions.
highlights.whyItMatters: A very common sign-error trap in torque/angular-momentum MCQs.

highlights.text: For rotation of a rigid body about a fixed axis, every particle's linear velocity is v = ω × r, where r is measured from any point on the axis; v is tangent to the particle's circular path and perpendicular to both ω and r.
highlights.whyItMatters: Bridges angular and linear kinematics for any particle of a rotating rigid body — foundational for all rolling/rotation problems.

highlights.text: Moment of force (torque) about a point: τ = r × F. Its magnitude is τ = rF sinθ = r_⊥F, where r_⊥ = r sinθ is the perpendicular distance of the line of action of F from the origin (also called the moment arm).
highlights.whyItMatters: Direct-recall definition; explains why force applied along the hinge line of a door produces zero torque.

highlights.text: Angular momentum of a particle about a point: l = r × p. Differentiating, dl/dt = τ — the rotational analogue of F = dp/dt. For a system, dL/dt = τ_ext, since internal torques cancel in equal-and-opposite pairs (Newton's third law, forces along the line joining the particles).
highlights.whyItMatters: Sets up the conservation law below; a required derivation-type question in board/competitive exams.

highlights.text: Conservation of angular momentum: if the total external torque on a system is zero, L = constant. Classic demonstrations: a skater or acrobat spins faster when pulling their arms/legs closer to the body (I decreases, so ω increases to keep L=Iω fixed); a spinning top and an oscillating table fan illustrate rotation about a fixed point versus a fixed line.
highlights.whyItMatters: One of the most frequently tested conceptual + numerical ideas in this chapter (ballet dancer/ice-skater question is a NEET perennial).

highlights.text: A rigid body is in mechanical equilibrium only if BOTH conditions hold: (1) translational equilibrium, ΣF_i = 0, and (2) rotational equilibrium, Στ_i = 0. A body can be in partial equilibrium — e.g. a couple has zero net force (so it satisfies translational equilibrium) but non-zero net torque, so it rotates without any translation.
highlights.whyItMatters: Distinguishes translational vs rotational equilibrium — a frequent assertion-reason trap (zero force does NOT imply zero torque, and vice versa).

highlights.text: Principle of moments for a lever: d₁F₁ = d₂F₂ (load-arm × load = effort-arm × effort). The Mechanical Advantage M.A. = F₁/F₂ = d₂/d₁; M.A. > 1 means a small effort can lift a large load.
highlights.whyItMatters: Direct numerical formula for lever/see-saw/beam-balance problems.

highlights.text: The centre of gravity (CG) of a body is the point where the total gravitational torque on the body is zero. The CG coincides with the centre of mass whenever the gravitational field g does not vary from one part of the body to another (true for all everyday-sized objects).
highlights.whyItMatters: Clarifies CG vs CM are conceptually different but numerically identical except for extremely large bodies where g varies.

highlights.text: Moment of inertia I = Σm_i r_i², where r_i is the perpendicular distance of the i-th particle from the axis. I plays the role of mass in rotational motion: K = ½Iω² and τ=Iα. Unlike mass, I depends on the axis chosen, not just on the body itself.
highlights.whyItMatters: Central quantity of the whole chapter; every rotational-dynamics formula involves I.

highlights.text: The parallel axis theorem I = I_cm + Md² applies to ANY axis parallel to one through the centre of mass, for ANY shaped body (not just symmetric ones). d is the perpendicular distance between the two parallel axes.
highlights.whyItMatters: Most-used formula for finding I about a non-central axis (e.g. a rod pivoted at one end: I = ML²/12 + M(L/2)² = ML²/3).

highlights.text: For rolling without slipping, the velocity of the point of contact with the surface is instantaneously zero. The centre's speed v_cm = ωR and acceleration a_cm = αR. The total kinetic energy of a rolling body is the SUM of translational and rotational kinetic energy: K = ½Mv_cm² + ½I_cmω².
highlights.whyItMatters: The single most tested numerical idea of the chapter — races between rolling ring/disc/sphere down an incline depend entirely on this total-KE split via I_cm = Mk².

definitions.definition: The point at which the entire mass of a system may be considered concentrated for describing its translational motion; R = Σm_i r_i/M for a discrete system.
An idealised body with a perfectly definite and unchanging shape — the distance between any two particles of the body never changes, however large the forces on it.
a×b is a vector c with magnitude ab sinθ, perpendicular to the plane of a and b, with direction given by the right-hand screw rule; it is NOT commutative, a×b = −(b×a).
The rotational analogue of force: τ = r × F, magnitude τ = rF sinθ = r_⊥F. Its SI unit is the newton metre (N m) — dimensionally the same as energy but a distinct vector quantity.
The rotational analogue of linear momentum: l = r × p for a particle; for a system, L = Σ(r_i × p_i). Its SI unit is kg m² s⁻¹ (equivalently J s).
A pair of equal and opposite forces with different lines of action, applied to a rigid body. A couple produces rotation without translation — net force zero, net torque non-zero.
The point of an extended body where the total gravitational torque is zero; coincides with the centre of mass when g is uniform over the body.
I = Σm_i r_i² — the rotational analogue of mass, characterising a body's resistance to a change in its rotational motion about a specific axis; depends on the mass distribution AND the chosen axis.
The distance from the axis at which the whole mass of the body could be concentrated to give the same moment of inertia; defined by I = Mk².

A disc-shaped rotating machine part with a deliberately large moment of inertia, used to resist sudden speed changes and provide a smooth, gradual change in rotational speed (e.g. steam/automobile engines).
A combination of translation and rotation in which the point of contact between the rolling body and the surface is instantaneously at rest; v_cm = ωR.

formulas.name: Centre of mass
formulas.latex: \vec{R} = \dfrac{\sum m_i \vec{r}_i}{M}, \qquad X=\dfrac{1}{M}\int x\,dm,\ Y=\dfrac{1}{M}\int y\,dm,\ Z=\dfrac{1}{M}\int z\,dm
formulas.plain: position of the centre of mass = mass-weighted average position of all particles (discrete sum, or integral for a continuous body)

symbols.meaning: mass and position vector of the i-th particle

formulas.whenToUse: Locating the effective point for translational motion of any discrete system or continuous rigid body; for uniform symmetric bodies (rod, ring, disc, sphere) it is simply the geometric centre by symmetry.
commonMistakes: Assuming the centre of mass always lies inside the material of the body — it can lie outside for a ring, L-shape or horseshoe.
Forgetting to use PERPENDICULAR (⊥) distances for continuous-body integrals when symmetry allows a shortcut instead.

questionPatterns.patternName: Locate CM of a discrete 2-3 particle system
questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Set up coordinates, list each mass and its position, apply the weighted-average formula per axis.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: Find the centre of mass of three particles of masses 100 g, 150 g and 200 g placed at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side 0.5 m.

questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Split the lamina into simple shapes (squares/rectangles), treat each piece's mass as concentrated at its own geometric centre.
questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: Apply X=Σm_ix_i/Σm_i, Y=Σm_iy_i/Σm_i using the sub-shapes' centres as the 'particles'.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: Find the centre of mass of a uniform L-shaped lamina (three 1 m × 1 m squares) of total mass 3 kg.

formulas.audioScript: Think of centre of mass as a weighted average position — each particle's location gets weighted by how much mass it carries. For symmetric uniform shapes, this always lands exactly at the geometric centre, but for a composite or oddly-shaped body you split it into simple pieces first.

formulas.name: Motion of the centre of mass / momentum of a system
formulas.plain: total mass × acceleration of CM = total external force; total momentum is conserved when external force is zero

symbols.meaning: acceleration and velocity of the centre of mass
total linear momentum of the system

formulas.whenToUse: Any system of particles/rigid body under external forces, INCLUDING cases with internal explosions, collisions or radioactive decay where internal forces are large but irrelevant to the CM's motion.
commonMistakes: Trying to track individual fragment trajectories after an explosion instead of just the simpler CM motion, which is unaffected by the internal explosion forces.
Forgetting this needs ONLY external forces — internal action-reaction pairs cancel out completely and contribute nothing to Eq. 6.11.

questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Recognize the explosion/decay forces are entirely internal, so the CM continues exactly as if nothing happened.
questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: The CM keeps following the original trajectory (e.g. the same parabola) since F_ext (gravity) is unchanged by the internal explosion.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: A projectile explodes mid-air into two fragments of unequal mass. Describe the subsequent motion of the centre of mass of the fragments.

questionPatterns.patternName: Person walking on a frictionless trolley
questionPatterns.howToInterpret: With F_ext=0 horizontally (frictionless floor), the CM of (person+trolley) stays fixed even as the person moves relative to the trolley.
questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: Use m₁Δx₁ + m₂Δx₂ = 0 (CM displacement zero) to relate the trolley's shift to the person's own displacement.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: A child of mass 20 kg sits at one end of a 10 kg trolley moving at speed V on a smooth floor. If the child gets up and walks to the other end, what happens to the speed of the CM of the (child+trolley) system?

formulas.audioScript: This is Newton's second law scaled up to a whole system — no matter how complicated the internal forces are, whether it's an explosion, a collision, or people walking around inside, the centre of mass only cares about the NET EXTERNAL force. If that's zero, momentum is conserved and the CM just cruises along unaffected.

formulas.name: Vector (cross) product
formulas.plain: the vector product in component/determinant form; magnitude = ab sinθ, direction by the right-hand screw rule

symbols.meaning: angle between a and b (smaller angle, <180°)

formulas.whenToUse: Computing torque (τ=r×F) or angular momentum (l=r×p) when vectors are given in component (î,ĵ,k̂) form.
commonMistakes: Forgetting a×b = −(b×a) — order matters, unlike the dot product.
Sign errors expanding the determinant — always expand along the top row with alternating signs.

questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Set up the 3×3 determinant with î,ĵ,k̂ in the top row and the two vectors' components below.
questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: Expand the determinant to get the resultant vector.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: Find a×b where a = 3î−4ĵ+5k̂ and b = −2î+ĵ+3k̂.

formulas.audioScript: The determinant trick is the fastest way to compute a cross product by hand — write î, ĵ, k̂ on top, the first vector's components in the middle row, the second vector's in the bottom row, then expand like any 3×3 determinant.

formulas.name: Linear velocity of a particle in rigid-body rotation
formulas.plain: linear velocity = angular velocity × position vector (from a point on the axis)

symbols.meaning: angular velocity vector, directed along the fixed axis
position vector of the particle from the axis

formulas.whenToUse: Relating the speed of any point of a spinning rigid body to its distance from the axis; foundation of rolling-motion problems.
commonMistakes: Using the position vector from the wrong origin — for rotation about a fixed axis with one point also fixed, r must be measured from that fixed point, not from the axis's foot alone.

questionPatterns.patternName: Speed of a point at radius r on a rotating body
questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Since ω⊥r for a fixed axis, |v| = ωr directly.
questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: v = ωr for points at perpendicular distance r from the axis; points ON the axis (r=0) are stationary.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: A wheel of radius 0.5 m rotates at 10 rad/s. Find the linear speed of a point on its rim and a point midway between the centre and the rim.

formulas.audioScript: Every particle of a spinning rigid body shares the same angular velocity ω, but their linear speeds scale with how far they are from the axis — v=ωr — which is exactly what the cross product v=ω×r captures automatically, including direction.

formulas.name: Torque (moment of force)
formulas.plain: torque = position vector × force; magnitude = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action

symbols.meaning: perpendicular distance of the line of action of F from the origin (moment arm)

formulas.whenToUse: Any problem about the turning/rotating effect of a force — door-opening, spanner, lever, rigid-body equilibrium problems.
commonMistakes: Using r (the full distance) instead of r_⊥=r sinθ (perpendicular distance) when computing magnitude by the scalar formula.
Forgetting torque is zero when F passes through the chosen origin/pivot (θ=0° or r=0).

questionPatterns.patternName: Torque of a given force about the origin
questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Identify r (position vector of the point of application) and F, then take the cross product.
questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: τ = r × F, evaluated via the determinant method (see F3).
questionPatterns.exampleStem: Find the torque of a force 7î+3ĵ−5k̂ about the origin, acting on a particle at position î−ĵ+k̂.

formulas.audioScript: Torque only cares about the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line along which the force acts — that's why pushing a door far from its hinges, at right angles to it, gives you the most turning effect for the least force.

formulas.name: Angular momentum of a particle; dl/dt = τ
formulas.plain: angular momentum = position vector × linear momentum; its rate of change equals the torque
formulas.whenToUse: The rotational analogue of F=dp/dt — used to derive angular momentum conservation and to find l directly for a particle in circular or general motion.
commonMistakes: Forgetting l need not be along the rotation axis for a general particle — only for symmetric rigid bodies rotating about a symmetry axis does L align with ω.

questionPatterns.patternName: Show angular momentum is conserved for straight-line motion at constant velocity
questionPatterns.howToInterpret: For a particle moving in a straight line, the perpendicular distance from any point O to the line (OM = r sinθ) stays constant even though r and θ individually change.
questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: l = mvr sinθ = mv×(constant perpendicular distance) = constant, and since v is constant and there's no external torque, l stays constant.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: Show that the angular momentum of a particle moving with constant velocity, about any fixed point, remains constant throughout its motion.

formulas.audioScript: This is the rotational twin of Newton's second law — instead of force changing momentum, torque changes angular momentum. If there's no torque about a point, angular momentum about that point simply cannot change.

formulas.name: Angular momentum for a system; conservation of angular momentum
formulas.plain: total angular momentum's rate of change equals only the external torque (internal torques cancel in pairs); if external torque is zero, L is conserved

symbols.meaning: total angular momentum of the system about a chosen point

formulas.whenToUse: Any system with no external torque about the chosen axis — spinning skaters/divers, planets in orbit, collapsing/expanding rotating systems.
commonMistakes: Confusing conservation of L (needs τ_ext=0) with conservation of linear momentum P (needs F_ext=0) — these are independent conditions; a couple has F_ext=0 but τ_ext≠0.
Forgetting L conservation for a symmetric rigid body about its symmetry axis becomes Iω=constant, which is what lets I and ω trade off against each other.

questionPatterns.patternName: Skater/diver pulling in arms and legs
questionPatterns.howToInterpret: No external torque about the spin axis ⟹ L=Iω is conserved; pulling arms in reduces I, so ω must increase.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: A ballet dancer spinning with her arms outstretched has moment of inertia 5 kg m² and angular speed 2 rad/s. If she pulls her arms in to reduce her moment of inertia to 2 kg m², find her new angular speed.

formulas.audioScript: Whenever there's no twisting force acting from outside, the total angular momentum is locked in — so if a spinning body somehow rearranges its own mass to have a smaller moment of inertia, its spin rate must shoot up to compensate, exactly like a figure skater pulling in their arms.

formulas.name: Equilibrium of a rigid body
formulas.plain: a rigid body is in mechanical equilibrium only if the net external force AND the net external torque are both zero
formulas.whenToUse: Ladders, beams, rods on knife-edges/supports, hinged doors — any statics problem with a rigid body at rest.
commonMistakes: Checking only one of the two conditions (force OR torque) — both must hold for full mechanical equilibrium; a body can be in translational equilibrium but NOT rotational (a couple), or vice versa is impossible unless forces are concurrent.
Forgetting the choice of pivot point for taking moments is arbitrary IF the body is already in translational equilibrium — but a poor choice makes the algebra harder, not wrong.

questionPatterns.patternName: Rod/beam on two supports with a load
questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Apply ΣF=0 vertically to relate the two support reactions, then Στ=0 about one support to solve for each reaction individually.
questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: R₁+R₂=W+W_load (translational); take moments about one knife-edge to eliminate one unknown reaction.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: A uniform 70 cm, 4 kg metal bar rests on two knife-edges placed 10 cm from each end, with a 6 kg load hung 30 cm from one end. Find the reaction forces at the two knife-edges.

questionPatterns.patternName: Ladder leaning against a frictionless wall
questionPatterns.howToInterpret: The wall (frictionless) can only push horizontally; the floor supplies both a normal reaction and friction; use both equilibrium conditions.
questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: ΣF_x=0, ΣF_y=0, and Στ=0 about the foot of the ladder (this eliminates the unknown floor reactions from the torque equation).
questionPatterns.exampleStem: A 3 m ladder weighing 20 kg leans against a frictionless wall, its foot 1 m from the wall on a rough floor. Find the reaction forces of the wall and the floor.

formulas.audioScript: Statics problems always need two separate equations — one from balancing forces, one from balancing torques — because a body can easily have zero net force while still wanting to spin, or vice versa. Choosing WHERE to take torques cleverly, usually at an unknown-reaction point, is the trick that makes the algebra manageable.

formulas.name: Principle of moments (lever) and centre of gravity
formulas.plain: load-arm × load = effort-arm × effort; mechanical advantage = effort arm / load arm; centre of gravity is where total gravity torque vanishes
formulas.whenToUse: Levers, see-saws, beam balances, and finding the CG of an irregular body by suspension from different points.
commonMistakes: Mixing up which arm goes with load vs effort in the M.A. ratio — M.A. = effort arm/load arm, so a LONGER effort arm gives GREATER mechanical advantage.
Assuming CG always equals CM — true only when g is uniform over the body, which holds for all everyday objects but not for astronomically large bodies.

questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Identify the fulcrum, then set load-arm×load equal to effort-arm×effort.
questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: d₁F₁=d₂F₂; solve for the unknown force or distance.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: A see-saw has a 20 kg child sitting 1.5 m from the pivot. Where must a 25 kg child sit on the other side to balance it?

formulas.audioScript: A lever is just a torque-balance problem in disguise — the load's turning effect on one side must exactly cancel the effort's turning effect on the other, which is why a longer effort arm lets a small force lift a much larger load.

formulas.name: Moment of inertia and radius of gyration
formulas.latex: I=\sum_i m_i r_i^2, \qquad I = Mk^2 \ \text{(defines radius of gyration } k\text{)}, \qquad I=I_{cm}+Md^2 \ \text{(parallel axis theorem)}
formulas.plain: moment of inertia = Σ(mass × perpendicular-distance²); radius of gyration k satisfies I=Mk²; parallel axis theorem shifts I to a parallel axis

symbols.meaning: distance between the parallel axis and the axis through the CM

formulas.whenToUse: Any rotational-dynamics or rolling problem — first step is almost always finding I about the relevant axis, often via the parallel axis theorem plus Table 6.1's standard results.
commonMistakes: Using the standard-body I formula (about the CM axis) directly when the actual axis is NOT through the CM — must add Md² via the parallel axis theorem first.
Confusing radius of gyration k (depends on axis, like I) with the body's actual geometric radius R (fixed property of the shape).

questionPatterns.patternName: I of a rod about its end (not centre)
questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Start from the standard result about the CM (perpendicular axis at midpoint), then shift using the parallel axis theorem.
questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: I_end = I_cm + Md² = ML²/12 + M(L/2)² = ML²/3.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: Find the moment of inertia of a uniform rod of mass M and length L about an axis perpendicular to the rod through one end.

questionPatterns.patternName: Balancing a metre stick with unequal added masses
questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Not a rotational-inertia question per se, but uses the same idea as centre of mass/torque balance — find where two added point masses plus the stick's own CG combine to a new balance point.
questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: Treat the stick's own weight as acting at its 50 cm mark, add torque contributions of the coins, and set the total torque about the new balance point to zero.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: A metre stick is balanced on a knife edge at its centre. When two 5 g coins are placed one on top of the other at the 12 cm mark, the stick balances at 45 cm. Find the mass of the metre stick.

formulas.audioScript: Moment of inertia is never a fixed property of a body the way mass is — it depends entirely on which axis you spin it about, which is exactly why the parallel axis theorem is so heavily used: it lets you shift a known result from the easy central axis to whatever axis the problem actually needs.

formulas.name: Rotational kinematics and dynamics (fixed axis)
formulas.latex: \omega=\omega_0+\alpha t,\quad \theta=\omega_0 t+\tfrac12\alpha t^2,\quad \omega^2=\omega_0^2+2\alpha\theta; \qquad \tau=I\alpha,\quad W=\tau\Delta\theta,\quad P=\tau\omega,\quad K=\tfrac12 I\omega^2
formulas.plain: the exact rotational analogues of the linear kinematics/dynamics equations, with θ↔x, ω↔v, α↔a, I↔M, τ↔F
formulas.whenToUse: Any fixed-axis rotation with constant angular acceleration (flywheels, motors, wheels speeding up/slowing down uniformly) — solve exactly like a 1D kinematics problem, just relabelling the symbols.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to convert rev/min to rad/s (× 2π/60) before substituting into these equations.
Using τ=Iα with a torque that isn't the NET external torque along the fixed axis — only axis-aligned torque components matter for fixed-axis rotation.

questionPatterns.patternName: Angular acceleration and revolutions of a speeding-up wheel
questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Convert given rpm values to rad/s, then apply the rotational kinematics equations exactly as in 1D linear kinematics.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: The angular speed of a motor wheel increases from 1200 rpm to 3120 rpm in 16 s. Find its angular acceleration and the number of revolutions it makes in that time.

questionPatterns.patternName: Work-energy on a flywheel pulled by a cord
questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Use τ=Iα to get α, then either the work-energy theorem (W=ΔK) or direct kinematics to connect angular displacement, work done, and final KE.
questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: τ=FR=Iα; W=Fd (linear, on the cord) should equal K=½Iω² gained (no friction).
questionPatterns.exampleStem: A 20 kg, 20 cm-radius flywheel on a frictionless axle is pulled by a steady 25 N force via a cord wound on its rim. Find the angular acceleration, work done as 2 m of cord unwinds, and the kinetic energy gained.

formulas.audioScript: Once you notice the exact one-to-one correspondence with ordinary straight-line kinematics — angle instead of distance, angular velocity instead of speed — every equation you already know for constant acceleration transfers over unchanged, just with new symbols.

formulas.name: Rolling motion
formulas.latex: v_{cm}=\omega R, \qquad a_{cm}=\alpha R, \qquad K_{total}=\tfrac12 M v_{cm}^2 + \tfrac12 I_{cm}\omega^2
formulas.plain: for rolling without slipping, the centre's speed equals ωR; total kinetic energy is translational PLUS rotational
formulas.whenToUse: Any ring/disc/cylinder/sphere rolling without slipping — down an incline, or with a given speed on a level surface.
commonMistakes: Using only ½Mv² (ignoring rotational KE) or only ½Iω² (ignoring translational KE) — rolling KE is always the SUM of both.

Forgetting that different bodies (ring, disc, sphere) with the same mass and radius reach the bottom of an incline at different times/speeds because their I_cm = Mk² differs — a race down a ramp is not a tie.

questionPatterns.patternName: Ratio of translational to rotational KE for a rolling body
questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Write I_cm = Mk² (using the standard-body result), then form the ratio using v=ωR.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: A solid sphere rolls without slipping. Find the ratio of its translational kinetic energy to its rotational kinetic energy.

questionPatterns.patternName: Speed of a rolling body at the bottom of an incline
questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Use energy conservation: loss in PE = total KE gained (translational + rotational), with v=ωR eliminating ω.
questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: Mgh = ½Mv²(1 + k²/R²), solve for v.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: A solid cylinder of mass M and radius R rolls without slipping down an incline of height h. Find its speed at the bottom, and compare it with the speed of a solid sphere of the same mass and radius released from the same height.

formulas.audioScript: Rolling motion always splits its kinetic energy budget into two pots — one for the centre of mass moving forward, one for the spin about that centre — and how that budget splits between the two pots depends entirely on the body's shape through its radius of gyration, which is exactly why a solid sphere always beats a hollow ring down the same ramp.

stages.question: Does the centre of mass of a body always lie within the material of the body?
stages.interpretation: Tests the misconception that CM must be 'inside' the object.
solutionSteps: Consider a uniform ring or an L-shaped lamina
By symmetry, the CM of a ring is at its centre — empty space, not material
So the CM can lie outside the body's material
stages.answer: No — e.g. a ring's centre of mass is at its centre, which is empty space, not part of the ring itself.

flashcards.audioScript: The centre of mass is a purely geometric/mass-weighted point — it has no obligation to sit on actual material, as a ring or a horseshoe shape makes obvious.

stages.question: Find a×b where a=3î−4ĵ+5k̂ and b=−2î+ĵ+3k̂.

flashcards.audioScript: Expand the 3×3 determinant with î, ĵ, k̂ on top — remember the middle (ĵ) term picks up a minus sign from the cofactor expansion.

stages.question: Find the torque about the origin of a force 7î+3ĵ−5k̂ acting on a particle at position î−ĵ+k̂.

flashcards.audioScript: Same determinant method as any cross product — just plug r and F into the middle and bottom rows in that order, since order matters for torque's sign.

stages.question: A couple acts on a rigid body. Is the body in translational equilibrium? Is it in rotational equilibrium?
stages.interpretation: Tests the independence of the two equilibrium conditions.
solutionSteps: A couple = two equal, opposite, parallel forces with different lines of action
Net force = 0, so YES translational equilibrium
Net torque ≠ 0 (both moments add, don't cancel), so NO rotational equilibrium
stages.answer: Yes translational equilibrium (net force zero); No rotational equilibrium (net torque non-zero) — the body undergoes pure rotation.

flashcards.audioScript: A couple is the textbook example that these two equilibrium conditions are completely independent — you can have zero net force while the body still spins, because the two forces' torques add instead of cancelling.

stages.question: A ballet dancer spinning with arms outstretched has I=5 kg m² and ω=2 rad/s. She pulls her arms in, reducing I to 2 kg m². Find her new angular speed.
stages.interpretation: No external torque about the spin axis, so L=Iω is conserved.

flashcards.audioScript: Since nothing external is twisting her, Iω must stay fixed — shrink the moment of inertia and the angular speed has to grow to compensate, exactly proportionally.

stages.question: Find the moment of inertia of a uniform rod of mass M and length L about an axis perpendicular to the rod through one end.
stages.interpretation: Shift the standard central-axis result using the parallel axis theorem.
solutionSteps: d = L/2 (distance from midpoint to end)
I_end = ML²/12 + M(L/2)² = ML²/12 + ML²/4 = ML²/3

flashcards.audioScript: Always start from the easy central-axis value from the standard-bodies table, then shift outward using the parallel axis theorem — here that turns ML²/12 into ML²/3, three times bigger.

stages.question: A see-saw has a 20 kg child sitting 1.5 m from the pivot. Where must a 25 kg child sit on the other side to balance it?
stages.interpretation: Principle of moments — load arm × load = effort arm × effort.

flashcards.audioScript: Balance the two turning effects directly — the heavier child needs a proportionally shorter arm to produce the same torque as the lighter child farther out.

stages.question: A uniform 70 cm, 4 kg metal bar rests on two knife-edges 10 cm from each end. A 6 kg load hangs 30 cm from the left end. Find the reactions R₁ (left) and R₂ (right). (g=9.8 m/s²)
stages.interpretation: Two-equation statics problem: force balance plus torque balance about one knife-edge.
solutionSteps: Knife edges at 10 cm and 60 cm from left end; centre G at 35 cm; load at 30 cm (5 cm left of G)
Taking moments about G: R₂ acts 25 cm right of G, R₁ acts 25 cm left of G, load acts 5 cm left of G
Solving with R₁+R₂=98.0: R₁≈54.9 N, R₂≈43.1 N

flashcards.audioScript: The key move in any beam-on-two-supports problem is picking a smart pivot point for the torque equation — usually the body's own centre of gravity or one of the supports — so that one of the two unknown reactions drops out of that equation entirely.

stages.question: A solid sphere and a hollow ring, of the same mass and radius, are released from rest from the same height on a frictionless-for-sliding-but-rolling-without-slipping incline. Which reaches the bottom first, and why?
stages.interpretation: Compare their final speeds using energy conservation with different k²/R² ratios.
solutionSteps: Sphere's v² is larger ⟹ sphere accelerates faster and reaches the bottom first
stages.answer: The solid sphere reaches the bottom first — a smaller k²/R² means less of the available energy is 'used up' spinning it, leaving more for forward speed.

flashcards.audioScript: The smaller a body's radius of gyration relative to its actual radius, the less of its gravitational PE gets diverted into spin, and the faster it accelerates down the slope — which is why a solid sphere always beats a hollow ring in this classic race, regardless of their common mass or radius.

conceptWarmup: Why can the centre of mass of a body lie outside the material of the body itself?
Why is the vector product NOT commutative, unlike the ordinary scalar product?
Why can a rigid body be in translational equilibrium (zero net force) but NOT in rotational equilibrium?

basic.question: Find the centre of mass of three particles of masses 100 g, 150 g and 200 g placed at (0,0), (0.5,0) and (0.25, 0.25√3) m respectively.
basic.interpretation: Direct weighted-average CM calculation for a discrete system.
basic.audioScript: Apply the weighted-average formula separately along x and y — each mass pulls the centre of mass toward itself in proportion to how heavy it is.

basic.question: A wheel of radius 0.5 m rotates at 10 rad/s. Find the linear speed of a point on the rim.
basic.interpretation: Direct v=ωr application at the rim.
basic.audioScript: Just multiply the angular speed by the radius — this is the most direct application of the angular-to-linear velocity relation.

basic.question: The angular speed of a motor wheel increases from 1200 rpm to 3120 rpm in 16 s. Find its angular acceleration.
basic.interpretation: Convert rpm to rad/s, then use the constant-α rotational kinematics equation.
basic.audioScript: Convert both speeds to rad/s first — this is the single most common place to lose marks in this type of problem — then it's a one-line subtraction divided by time.

intermediate.question: A child of mass 20 kg sits at one end of a 10 kg, 2 m long trolley at rest on a frictionless floor. The child walks to the other end. How far does the trolley move?
intermediate.interpretation: External horizontal force is zero, so the CM of (child+trolley) stays fixed even as the child moves relative to the trolley.
steps: Let the trolley shift by d (opposite to the child's motion relative to ground)
CM-fixed condition: 20(2−d) = 10×d (child's displacement relative to ground vs trolley's)
Actually use: m_child × (child's ground displacement) = −m_trolley × d, with child's ground displacement = (2−d)
intermediate.answer: The trolley shifts back by 4/3 ≈ 1.33 m (child moves forward by 2−4/3 = 2/3 m relative to ground)
intermediate.audioScript: Even though the child physically walks the trolley's whole 2 m length relative to the trolley, the combined centre of mass can't move at all — so the trolley itself must slide backward to compensate, in inverse proportion to the two masses.

intermediate.question: Find the centre of mass of a uniform L-shaped lamina made of three 1 m × 1 m squares (as in NCERT Fig. 6.11), total mass 3 kg.
intermediate.interpretation: Split into 3 unit squares, each 1 kg concentrated at its own geometric centre.
steps: Squares centred at (0.5,0.5), (1.5,0.5), (0.5,1.5) [one possible L layout], each mass 1 kg
intermediate.answer: (5/6, 5/6) m — lies on the diagonal line of symmetry of the L-shape, NOT inside the 'missing' corner square
intermediate.audioScript: Split any composite shape into simple pieces you already know the centre of mass of, treat each piece's mass as if concentrated at its own centre, and average — this is exactly how the NCERT L-lamina example works.

intermediate.question: Find the ratio of translational to rotational kinetic energy for a solid cylinder rolling without slipping.
intermediate.interpretation: Use I_cm=MR²/2 for a solid cylinder, then form the KE ratio using v=ωR.
intermediate.answer: 2 : 1 (translational KE is twice the rotational KE for a solid cylinder)
intermediate.audioScript: This ratio only depends on the shape's radius of gyration relative to its radius — for a solid cylinder that ratio works out to a clean 2:1 split in favour of translation.

advanced.question: A 3 m ladder weighing 20 kg leans against a frictionless wall, its foot 1 m from the wall on a rough floor. Find the reaction forces of the wall and the floor. (g=9.8 m/s²)
advanced.interpretation: Full rigid-body statics: translational equilibrium in both directions plus rotational equilibrium about the foot.
steps: Torque about foot A: F₁(2√2) = W(0.5) [W acts at midpoint, 0.5 m horizontal from foot]
Total floor reaction F₂=√(F²+N²)=√(34.6²+196²)≈199.0 N, at angle tan⁻¹(196/34.6)≈80° to horizontal
advanced.answer: Wall reaction ≈ 34.6 N (horizontal); Floor reaction ≈ 199.0 N at ≈80° to the horizontal (NCERT Example 6.9)
advanced.audioScript: Take torques about the ladder's foot specifically, since that makes both unknown floor-reaction components drop out of the torque equation entirely, leaving a single equation for the wall's reaction alone.

advanced.question: A cord of negligible mass is wound round a 20 kg, 20 cm-radius flywheel on a frictionless axle. A steady 25 N pull is applied. Find (a) the angular acceleration, (b) work done as 2 m of cord unwinds, (c) the kinetic energy gained, assuming it starts from rest.
advanced.interpretation: Chain τ=Iα for angular acceleration, then either direct work W=Fd or the rotational work-energy route, to show both give the same KE.
steps: Work by the pull = F×d = 25×2 = 50 J
K=½Iω²=½×0.4×250=50 J — matches the work done, confirming no energy loss
advanced.answer: α=12.5 rad/s²; Work=50 J; KE gained=50 J (equal, since the axle is frictionless)
advanced.audioScript: This problem is really a check that the work-energy theorem holds for rotation just as it does for translation — every joule of work done unwinding the cord shows up exactly as kinetic energy of the spinning flywheel, with nothing lost to friction.

advanced.question: A solid cylinder of mass M and radius R rolls without slipping down an incline of height h, starting from rest. Find its speed at the bottom, and compare with a solid sphere of the same mass and radius released from the same height.
advanced.interpretation: Energy conservation with rolling KE split between translation and rotation, parameterised by k²/R² for each shape.
steps: Compare: 4/3≈1.333 vs 10/7≈1.429 — sphere's v² coefficient is larger
advanced.answer: v_cylinder=√(4gh/3); v_sphere=√(10gh/7) — the sphere is faster because more of its available energy goes into translation (smaller k²/R²)
advanced.audioScript: Neither mass nor radius actually matters for who wins this race — only the shape's k²/R² ratio does, since it alone decides what fraction of the falling energy is diverted from forward motion into spin.

problemLadder.transferPrompt: After finishing the ladder, invent one NEET-style MCQ that combines conservation of angular momentum (a spinning platform) with the parallel axis theorem (a person moving their arms changes I about the spin axis), and one that connects the rolling-motion energy split here with the earlier Work-Energy chapter's KE formula.

Start by asking whether I want to revise definitions, practice numericals, or focus on a weak sub-topic (centre of mass & momentum of a system, vector products, torque & angular momentum, equilibrium & centre of gravity, moment of inertia, rotational kinematics/dynamics, or rolling motion). First quiz me on definitions and formulas with NO calculation involved — centre of mass vs centre of gravity, torque vs angular momentum, translational vs rotational equilibrium, and moment of inertia vs radius of gyration. Then move to basic numericals tied to a single formula (locating a CM, v=ωr, torque of a given force, rotational kinematics). Then intermediate problems requiring two steps (composite-lamina CM, angular momentum conservation for a spinning skater, parallel-axis-theorem moment of inertia, lever/see-saw balance). Then advanced multi-stage problems (ladder-against-a-wall statics, rod-on-two-knife-edges statics, flywheel work-energy, rolling-body race down an incline). After every wrong answer, walk me through: (1) what is actually being asked (Interpretation), (2) which formula connects to it and why, (3) the solution steps, before revealing the final answer. Offer a flashcard mode (test me stage by stage: question → interpretation → formula → steps → answer) and a formula-view mode (list all 12 formulas with when-to-use notes). Stay within this chapter's scope (centre of mass, vector products, torque, angular momentum, equilibrium, moment of inertia, rotational kinematics/dynamics, rolling motion) unless I explicitly ask to connect to another chapter.

selfCheck.q: What two conditions must BOTH hold for a rigid body to be in mechanical equilibrium?
selfCheck.a: Zero net external force (translational equilibrium) AND zero net external torque (rotational equilibrium) — both are independently required.
I = I_cm + Md², where I_cm is the moment of inertia about a parallel axis through the centre of mass and d is the distance between the two parallel axes.

selfCheck.q: Under what condition is the total angular momentum of a system conserved?
selfCheck.a: When the total external torque acting on the system is zero — internal torques always cancel in equal-and-opposite pairs by Newton's third law.

selfCheck.q: Why does a solid sphere roll down an incline faster than a hollow ring of the same mass and radius?
selfCheck.a: The sphere has a smaller radius of gyration (k²/R²=2/5 vs 1 for the ring), so less of its gravitational PE is diverted into rotational KE, leaving more available for translational speed.

selfCheck.q: What is the total kinetic energy of a body rolling without slipping?
selfCheck.a: The SUM of translational and rotational kinetic energy: K = ½Mv_cm² + ½I_cmω², never just one term alone.
